title: Real estate · Rossi and Patel: appraisal-based index, REOC vs REIT, AFFO, NAV per share
body:
Marco Ricci is a financial adviser specializing in commercial real estate investing. He meets with Anita Shah, a new client, who wants to diversify her portfolio by adding real estate investments to it.

Using data from an appraisal-based index, Ricci discusses real estate return and risk statistics with Shah and compares them to the return and risk of Shah's current portfolio of stocks and bonds. Based on Shah's investment objectives, Ricci recommends the following types of investments: 

Investment 1: A real estate operating company (REOC);
Ιnvestment 2: An equity real estate investment trust (REIT).
Shah asks Ricci how REITs and REOCs are valued. Ricci mentions that the following measures are widely used in the valuation of REITs and REOCs: 
Measure 1: EBITDA;
Measure 2: Funds from operations (FFO);
Measure 3: Adjusted funds from operations (AFFO).
Next, Ricci presents Shah with the valuation of a REIT. REIT A is a multi-family REIT and its NAV is calculated based on the net operating income (NOI) information in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
 	REIT A
Property subsector	Multi-family
Last-12-month real estate NOI	$280,000
Last-12-month non-cash rent	$9,800
Last-12-month capital expenditures	$40,000
Cash and equivalents	$69,300
Total debt	$823,000
Discount rate	6.5%
Estimated growth rate	1.5%
Shares outstanding	50,000

questions.q: The type of index Ricci uses will most likely:
options: overstate the diversification benefits of real estate.
have values that lead the transaction values in the market.
introduce noise in the index measurement.
questions.why: A. Correct because Ricci uses an appraisal-based index, and appraisal-based indexes are often criticized for having appraisal lag, which results from appraised values tending to lag when there are sudden shifts in the market. Appraisal lag tends to smooth the index, meaning that it has less volatility. It behaves somewhat like a moving average of what an index would look like if it were based on values obtained from transactions rather than appraisals. Because of the lag in appraisal-based real estate indexes, they will also tend to have a lower correlation with other asset classes. The smoothing effect will also overstate Sharpe ratios, which is problematic if the index is used in asset allocation models to determine how much of a portfolio should be allocated to real estate versus other asset classes. The appropriate allocation to and benefits from private real estate would likely be overestimated. | B. Incorrect because appraisal-based indexes are often criticized for having appraisal lag, which results from appraised values tending to lag when there are sudden shifts in the market. In an upward market, transaction prices usually start to rise first. Then as these higher prices are reflected in comparable sales and investor surveys, they are captured in appraised values. Thus, appraisal-based indexes may not capture the price increase until a quarter or more after it was reflected in transactions. The same lag would also occur in a down market, with appraised values not falling as soon as transaction prices. Incorrect answer: (no answer) Correct Answer: overstate the diversification benefits of real estate. | C. Incorrect because this is a problem associated with transaction-based indexes, not appraisal-based indexes. Transaction-based indexes can be noisy (that is, they include random elements in the observations) because of the need to use statistical techniques to estimate the index. So, there may be upward or downward movements from quarter to quarter that are somewhat random even though in general (viewed over a year or longer) the index is capturing the correct movements in the market. On the other hand, appraisal-based indexes combine valuation information from individual properties and provide a measure of market movements.

questions.q: Compared to Investment 1 recommended by Ricci, Investment 2 most likely:
options: avoids double taxation on dividends received by investors.
is better able to hold properties under development.
requires less expertise in real estate investing.
questions.why: A. Correct because REIT and passthrough structures avoid corporate income taxation, leaving only the investor to pay taxes on dividends received. On the other hand, real estate operating companies are ordinary taxable real estate ownership companies. Businesses are organized as REOCs, as opposed to REITs, if they are located in countries that do not have a tax-advantaged REIT regime in place, if they engage to a large extent in the development of for-sale real estate properties, or if they offer other non-qualifying services, such as brokerage and third-party property management. Incorrect answer: (no answer) Correct Answer: avoids double taxation on dividends received by investors. | B. Incorrect because the relatively low rates of income retention that are required to maintain a REIT’s tax-free status can detract from income growth potential. In most countries, REITs are required to distribute 90%–100% of their otherwise taxable earnings, invest at least 75% of their assets in real estate, and derive at least 75% of income from real estate rental income or interest on mortgages. To engage in non-REIT-qualifying activities, such as merchant development, REITs form taxable REIT subsidiaries (TRS). On the other hand, real estate operating companies are ordinary taxable real estate ownership companies. Businesses are organized as REOCs, as opposed to REITs if they engage to a large extent in the development of for-sale real estate properties. | C. Incorrect because investment in publicly traded equity investments (in REITs or REOCs) requires much less expertise than private equity investments because investors benefit from having their property interests actively managed on their behalf by professional managers and from having their business interests overseen and guided by boards of directors, as in the case of all public corporations. Therefore, both types of investment provide access to professional management, limiting the required investor qualifications to equity investing generally.

questions.q: Which of the measures discussed by Ricci best reflects the dividend-paying ability of a REIT?
questions.why: A. Incorrect because EBITDA is not a cash-focused measure of current economic income. The purpose of the adjustments to net earnings made in computing FFO and AFFO is to obtain a more tangible, cash-focused measure of sustainable economic income that reduces reliance on non-cash accounting estimates and excludes non-economic, non-cash charges. | B. Incorrect because AFFO is more reflective of a REIT’s dividend-paying ability than FFO. Adjusted funds from operations, also known as funds available for distribution (FAD) or cash available for distribution, is a refinement of FFO that is designed to be a more accurate measure of current economic income. AFFO is most often defined as FFO adjusted to remove any non-cash rent and to subtract maintenance-type capital expenditures and leasing costs (including leasing agents’ commissions and tenants’ improvement allowances). | C. Correct because adjusted funds from operations, also known as funds available for distribution (FAD) or cash available for distribution, is a refinement of FFO that is designed to be a more accurate measure of current economic income. AFFO is most often defined as FFO adjusted to remove any non-cash rent and to subtract maintenance-type capital expenditures and leasing costs (including leasing agents’ commissions and tenants’ improvement allowances). AFFO is also more reflective of a REIT’s dividend-paying ability than FFO. Incorrect answer: (no answer) Correct Answer: Measure 3

questions.q: The NAV per share for REIT A is closest to:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because it incorrectly discounts next-12-month cash NOI as opposed to capping it (i.e., it uses the discount rate instead of the cap rate). Last-12-month NOI = $280,000 Less: Non-cash rents = $9,800 Last-12-month cash NOI = $270,200 Next-12-month growth in NOI = $270,200 × 1.5% = $4,053 Estimated next-12-month cash NOI = $270,200 + $4,053 = $274,253 Estimated value of operating real estate = Estimated next-12-month cash NOI/discount rate = $274,253/6.5% = $4,219,276.92. Plus: Cash and equivalents $69,300 Estimated gross asset value = $4,288,576.92 Less: Total debt = $823,000 Net asset value (NAV) = $3,465,576.92 NAV per share = $3,465,576.92/50,000 = $69.31. | B. Correct because the value of $94.63 is calculated as follows: Cap rate = discount rate – estimated growth rate = 6.5% – 1.5% = 5.0% Last-12-month NOI = $280,000 Less: Non-cash rents = $9,800 Last-12-month cash NOI = $270,200 Next-12-month growth in NOI = $270,200 × 1.5% = $4,053 Estimated next-12-month cash NOI = $270,200 + $4,053 = $274,253 Estimated value of operating real estate = Estimated next-12-month cash NOI/cap rate = $274,253/5.0% = $5,485,060. Estimated gross asset value = $5,554,360 Less: Total debt = $823,000 Net asset value (NAV) = $4,731,360 NAV per share = $4,731,360/50,000 = $94.63. Incorrect answer: (no answer) Correct Answer: $94.63. | C. Incorrect because it reduces last-12-month NOI by capital expenditure. However, the income return is not the same as cash flow, because cash flow is calculated after capital expenditures. That is, the amount of cash flow available each quarter is net operating income (or rental revenue less property operating expenses, including property taxes and insurance) minus capital expenditures. Cap rate = discount rate – estimated growth rate = 6.5% – 1.5% = 5.0% Last-12-month NOI = $280,000 Less: Non-cash rents = $9,800 Less: Last-12-month capital expenditures = $40,000 Last-12-month cash NOI = $230,200 Next-12-month growth in NOI = $230,200 × 1.5% = $3,453 Estimated next-12-month cash NOI = $230,200 + $3,453 = $233,653 Estimated value of operating real estate = Estimated next-12-month cash NOI/cap rate = $233,653/5.0% = $4,673,060. Estimated gross asset value = $4,742,360 Less: Total debt = $823,000 Net asset value (NAV) = $3,919,360 NAV per share = $3,919,360/50,000 = $78.39.

title: Active management · Mackie: three managers and the fundamental law
body:
Paula Maddison is a portfolio manager with a family office. She is reviewing the performance of three managers of active portfolios over the past year.

First, Maddison considers Manager 1's portfolio, which is invested in an equity fund and a fixed-income fund. Exhibit 1 shows Manager 1's strategic asset allocation and current allocation to these funds as well as the return on the two funds and their benchmarks.

Exhibit 1
 	Fund Return	Benchmark Return	Strategic Asset Allocation	Manager 1 Allocation
Equity fund	10.0%	12.0%	50%	60%
Fixed-income fund	3.0%	1.0%	50%	40%
Maddison meets with Manager 2, who runs an unconstrained global equities portfolio. Maddison informs Manager 2 that the family office will require ESG considerations to be incorporated into all of their investments going forward. The manager considers how the imposition of ESG constraints will affect portfolio performance as measured by the fundamental law of active management.

After her discussion with Manager 2, Maddison does further research into the strengths and limitations of the fundamental law of active management and makes the following observations:

Observation 1: If returns are not independent, the number of assets in a portfolio is not an adequate measure of breadth.
Observation 2: The fundamental law requires the empirical validity of the CAPM.
Lastly, Maddison gathers information about Manager 3's portfolio in Exhibit 2. She uses the fundamental law of active management to evaluate the portfolio's performance.

Exhibit 2
Information coefficient	0.09
Transfer coefficient	0.70
Breadth	9
Active portfolio risk	0.33

questions.q: The value added to Manager 1's portfolio attributable to security selection is closest to:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because it is Manager 1's portfolio return less the benchmark return, or the total value added (RA = RP – RB): [(0.6)(0.1) + (0.4)(0.03)] – [(0.5)(0.12) + (0.5)(0.01)] = 7.2% – 6.5% = 0.7%. It is also the sum of the value added by security selection and the value added by asset allocation: –0.4% + 1.1% = 0.7%. | B. Correct because the value added by security selection is the product of the active return (RA), which is the return on each underlying fund (RP) less the return on its respective benchmark (RB), and the allocated weight given to each fund, respectively. In this case: 0.6(0.10 – 0.12) + 0.4(0.03 – 0.01) = –1.2% + 0.8% = –0.4%. | C. Incorrect because it is the value added by asset allocation, not by security selection. Since the active weights are 60% to the Equity fund (compared with 50% for the Strategic Asset Allocation) and 40% to the Fixed-income fund (compared with 50% for the Strategic Asset Allocation), the value added from asset allocation is (60% – 50%)(0.12) + (40% – 50%)(0.01) = 1.2% – 0.1% = 1.1%.

questions.q: In terms of the fundamental law of active management, the family office's investment requirements will most likely lower Manager 2's:
questions.why: A. Correct because Manager 2's portfolio is currently unconstrained and therefore its transfer coefficient equals 1, the planned addition of ESG constraint would reduce this. Like the information coefficient, the transfer coefficient, TC, is a simple multiplicative factor in the fundamental law. It measures the extent to which constraints reduce the expected value added of the investor’s forecasting ability. In the absence of constraints, the transfer coefficient is approximately 1.00, resulting in the basic form of the fundamental law. However, in practice, investors often work under constraints that result in TC values between 0.20 and 0.80. | B. Incorrect because Manager 2 will be under the constraint of having fewer eligible securities available; the risk level he prefers to take with the available securities is not constrained. Active risk is "the volatility of the active return." | C. Incorrect because breadth measures the number of independent decisions; it is not affected by constraints on the fund. For example, despite fewer eligible stocks, if the manager increased the frequency of trading, it would increase the breadth.

questions.q: Are both of Maddison's observations about the fundamental law of active management correct?
questions.why: A. Incorrect because the fundamental law does not require the empirical validity of the CAPM. The fundamental law does not require the empirical validity of the CAPM, the multi-factor APT (arbitrage pricing theory), or any other equilibrium theory of required returns. | B. Correct because the number of individual assets, N, is not an adequate measure of strategy breadth, BR, when the active returns between individual assets are correlated, as defined by the risk model, and forecasts are not independent from period to period. Another example of the limitation of the fundamental law due to the lack of decision independence is the active management of fixed-income portfolios. Statement 2 is incorrect because the fundamental law does not require the empirical validity of the CAPM, the multi-factor APT (arbitrage pricing theory), or any other equilibrium theory of required returns. | C. Incorrect because Statement 2 is incorrect. The fundamental law does not require the empirical validity of the CAPM, the multi-factor APT (arbitrage pricing theory), or any other equilibrium theory of required returns.

questions.q: Based on the fundamental law of active management, Manager 3's information ratio is closest to:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because it is the expected active return, not the information ratio. The fundamental law states that E(RA) = (IC)(TC)(BR)0.5σA, where E(RA) is the expected active return, IC is the information coefficient, TC is the transfer coefficient, BR is the breadth, and σA is the active standard deviation. In this case E(RA) = (0.09)(0.7)(9)0.5(0.33) = 0.0624 ≈ 0.06. | B. Correct because the fundamental law states that E(RA) = (IC)(TC)(BR)0.5σA, where E(RA) is the expected active return, IC is the information coefficient, TC is the transfer coefficient, BR is the breadth, and σA is the active portfolio risk. Since the Information ratio is E(RA)/σA, from the above equation it can be shown that the IR = (IC)(TC)(BR)0.5 = (0.09)(0.7)(9)0.5 = 0.189 ≈ 0.19. | C. Incorrect because the square root of the breadth has been omitted, resulting in IR = (0.09)(0.7)(9) = 0.567 ≈ 0.57. This is also closest to the misinterpretation of the expected active return being (IC)(TC)(BR)0.5, leading to E(RA)/σA = [(0.09)(0.7)(9)0.5] / (0.33) = 0.5727 ≈ 0.57.

title: CDS · Marcos Pereira: Tundra Partners
body:
Marco Pinto is a credit analyst with Steppe Partners, a hedge fund manager. Steppe enters into single-name CDS for speculative purposes.  Pinto compiles information about Steppe’s CDS portfolio in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
 	Position	Coupon	Origination Credit Spread	Current Credit Spread
CDS 1	Protection Buyer	1.0%	75 bps	100 bps
CDS 2	Protection Seller	1.0%	100 bps	200 bps
CDS 3	Protection Seller	5.0%	650 bps	600 bps
CDS 4	Protection Seller	5.0%	450 bps	In default
CDS 1 and 2 relate to the same reference entity, and were entered into by Steppe on the same date. CDS 1 and 2 have a remaining time to maturity of 2 and 5 years respectively.

Exhibit 2
Maturity	Trading Price
Senior unsecured bond	3 years	30% of par
Senior unsecured bond	5 years	35% of par
Subordinated unsecured bond	8 years	20% of par
Pinto also whether Steppe should invest in CDS 5. He calculates that CDS 5’s reference entity has a hazard rate of 1.35% and 2.35% in each of the next 2 years.

Pinto notices that the market expects a local company to be the target of a leveraged buyout (LBO), whereby it will issue large amounts of debt and use the proceeds to repurchase its publicly traded equity. As a result, the credit spread of the company's senior unsecured bonds with 5 years until maturity has increased to 450 bps. A comparable 5-year CDS currently trades at a spread of 400 bps. Pinto believes that credit spreads in both markets should soon converge.

questions.q: When Steppe entered into CDS 1 and 2, its view about the reference entity's credit curve was most likely that the curve would:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because, as explained in the rationale for the correct answer, with CDS 1 and 2, Steppe entered into a curve trade expecting that the reference entity's credit curve would flatten, not remain unchanged. | B. Correct because entering into CDS 1 and 2 together constitute a curve trade, which involves buying single-name or index protection at one maturity and selling protection in the same reference entity at a different maturity. A steeper curve means that long-term credit risk increases relative to short term credit risk. An investor who believes that long-term credit risk will increase relative to short-term credit risk (credit curve steepening) can buy protection by buying a long-term single-name CDS and sell protection by selling a short-term single-name CDS. On the other hand, a flatter curve means that long-term credit risk decreases relative to short term credit risk.  An investor who believes that long-term credit risk will decrease relative to short-term credit risk (credit curve flattening) can sell protection by selling a long-term single-name CDS and buy protection by buying a short-term single-name CDS.  This is the case of the curve trade entered into by Steppe. Therefore, its view about the reference entity's credit curve was that it would flatten. | C. Incorrect because, as explained in the rationale for the correct answer, with CDS 1 and 2, Steppe entered into a curve trade expecting that the reference entity's credit curve would flatten, not steepen.

questions.q: If Steppe closes its position in CDS 3 today, it will:
options: pay an upfront premium and monetize a gain.
receive an upfront premium and monetize a gain.
pay an upfront premium and monetize a loss.
questions.why: A. Correct because if Steppe was to close its position in CDS 3, it will have to buy credit protection with a newly created CDS with a coupon of 5.0% and the same remaining maturity as CDS 3.  As the reference entity’s credit spread is currently 600 bps, to buy such credit protection, Steppe has to pay an upfront premium. However, as the reference entity’s credit spread decreased by 50 bps (i.e., credit quality improved) the upfront premium that Steppe has to pay is lower than the upfront premium it received at origination. Therefore, it will monetize a gain. | B. Incorrect because Steppe will pay an upfront premium and monetize a gain. | C. Incorrect because Steppe will pay an upfront premium and monetize a gain.

questions.q: Based on Pinto's analysis, the probability of default of CDS 5’s reference entity within the next 2 years is closest to:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because it incorrectly computes the probability of default of the entity in the next 2 years as the sum of the two hazard rates: Probability of default = 1.35% + 2.35% = 3.70% | B. Incorrect because it incorrectly computes the probability of default of the entity in the next 2 years as: Probability of default = [(1 +1.35%) x (1+ 2.35%) - 1]  = 3.73% | C. Correct because the probability of default of the entity in the next 2 years is computed as: Probability of default = 1 – Probability of Survival in the next 2 years whereas, Probability of survival in the next 2 years = (1 – hazard rate year 1) x (1 – hazard rate year 2) Probability of survival in the next 2 years = (1 – 1.35%) x (1 – 2.35%) = 96.33% Therefore, Probability of default = 1 – 96.33% = 3.67%

questions.q: Which of the following trades is consistent with Pinto's belief about the local company's credit spread convergence?
options: Buy bonds and sell CDS credit protection
Buy bonds and buy CDS credit protection
Sell bonds and buy CDS credit protection
questions.why: A. Incorrect because as explained in the rationale for the correct answer Steppe should buy bonds and buy credit protection. | B. Correct because the credit spread situation provide an opportunity for a basis trade.  Per the reading, the general idea behind most basis trades is that any such mispricing is likely to be temporary and the spreads in the bond and the CDS markets should return to equivalence when the market recognizes the disparity. For example, suppose the bond market implies a 4.5% credit risk premium whereas the CDS market implies a 4.0% credit risk premium. The trader does not know which is correct but believes these two rates will eventually converge. From the perspective of the CDS, its risk premium is too low relative to the bond credit risk premium. From the perspective of the bond, its risk premium is too high relative to the CDS market, which means its price is too low. So, the CDS market could be pricing in too little credit risk, and/or the bond market could be pricing in too much credit risk. Either market could be correct, it does not matter. The investor would buy the bond at a price that appears to overestimate its credit risk, and, at the same time, buy credit protection at what appears to be an unjustifiably low premium. If the convergence occurs, the trade would capture the 0.5% differential in the two markets. | C. Incorrect because as explained in the rationale for the correct answer Steppe should buy bonds and buy credit protection.

title: Marker: BR Hotels, ESG in corporate bonds
body:
Emma Marlowe, CFA, is a fixed-income analyst for the Hanbit Funds. Her supervisor asks her to identify ESG factors and value the corporate bonds of KT Hotels, a publicly traded boutique hotel company. Marlowe notes that KT Hotels is a “green hotel” company that prioritizes sustainability and has successfully reduced water and energy usage at its hotels. The founding family owns 55% of the outstanding shares. Each ownership share has equivalent voting rights.The board of directors of KT Hotels consists of 15 members, with independent CEO and chairperson roles. The board includes one independent member and two women, and 20% of the board members have experience in the hotel industry.

KT Hotels has historically had a high labor turnover rate. Most of its workforce are paid at or near the minimum wage, and the company offers no health benefits. Marlowe and her supervisor discuss how KT Hotels will be affected by the expected passage of legislation raising the minimum wage and growing pressure to offer benefits. Marlowe integrates ESG factors in the investment valuation of KT Hotels’ corporate bonds.

questions.q: The potential conflict between or among shareholders and managers of KT Hotels can best be described as:
questions.why:
C is correct. KT Hotels has concentrated ownership, given that the family owns 55% of the shares. It also has concentrated voting power, since each ownership share has equal voting rights. In this ownership structure, the controlling shareholders have power over both management and minority shareholders. The controlling shareholders are referred to as strong shareholders and the managers as weak managers. The conflict in this structure exists between the controlling shareholders and the minority shareholders. The controlling shareholders can potentially divert resources for their own benefit at the expense of the minority shareholders. This conflict is referred to as a principal-principal problem.

B is incorrect since the conflict for KT Hotels is a principal-principal problem. Voting caps are legal restrictions on the voting rights of large share positions. They result from an ownership structure of concentrated ownership and dispersed voting rights.

A is incorrect since the conflict for KT Hotels is a principal-principal problem. The principal-agent problem occurs when the ownership structure has dispersed ownership and dispersed voting rights. In this case, the structure has weak shareholders and strong management, with a potentially significant conflict between the shareholders and the management.

questions.q: KT Hotels’ corporate governance risk is increased by:
options: the low percentage of independent board members.
questions.why:
A is correct. The corporate governance risk for KT Hotels is high due to a low percentage of independent board members. Of the 15 members on the board, only one is independent. Many OECD countries have introduced a recommendation for the minimum ratio of independent directors serving on the board. They typically set the minimum ratio of independent directors in a range of 20%–50% or greater. KT Hotels falls below this range.

B is incorrect since CEO duality is not a governance problem for KT Hotels. KT Hotels’ CEO and chairperson are separate, so there is no CEO duality. This is typically a sign of effective corporate governance. The independent chairperson and CEO roles help protect investor interests.

C is incorrect because family control is not likely to increase governance risk for KT Hotels. Family control lowers the risks associated with principal-agent problems. This is the result of the family’s having concentrated ownership and management responsibility. The lower risk associated with the principal-agent problem is somewhat offset by the drawbacks of family control, which include poor transparency, modest considerations for minority shareholder rights, and difficulty in attracting quality management talent.

questions.q: The security analysis of KT Hotels is most likely focused on:
questions.why:
B is correct. The implementation of ESG factors in security analysis differs for equity analysis and fixed-income analysis. For BK Hotels’ corporate bonds, the focus of ESG integration is on mitigating downside risk. In contrast, in equity analysis, ESG integration is used to both identify potential opportunities and mitigate downside risk.

A is incorrect since adjusting the discount rate is typically used in equity analysis and not in fixed-income analysis. In valuing a stock, an analyst may choose to adjust the discount factor to account for the ESG risk. In fixed-income analysis, the credit spread or CDS is adjusted to reflect the ESG risk.

C is incorrect since identifying potential opportunities is used in equity analysis and not in fixed-income analysis. In fixed-income analysis, the focus of ESG integration is on mitigating downside risk. In equity analysis, ESG integration is used to both identify potential opportunities and mitigate downside risk.

questions.q: After integrating the ESG factors, the credit spread on KT Hotels’ bonds is most likely to:
questions.why:
A is correct. KT Hotels faces significant corporate governance and social risk. Corporate governance risk is high due to a low number of independent board members (1 out of 15 members), lack of gender diversity (2 women out of 15 members), and low percentage of board members with hotel industry experience (20%). These factors are likely to increase investors’ perception of the corporation’s risk. The social risk for KT Hotels is also high. KT Hotels has a high labor turnover rate, pays most of its workforce at or near the minimum wage, and offers no health benefits. Legislation raising the minimum wage and the growing pressure on KT Hotels to offer benefits would increase operating costs. This could have a negative impact on future cash flows, which would be detrimental to the bond holders. The valuation of KT Hotels’ bonds could be adversely affected by the higher ESG risk. To account for the higher ESG risk, the credit spread on KT Hotels’ bonds is likely to increase.

B is incorrect since the credit spread on KT Hotels’ bonds is likely to increase and not decrease.

C is incorrect since the credit spread on KT Hotels’ bonds is likely to increase and not remain unchanged.

title: Amaral and Mantri: institutions, capital deepening and Mali strategies
body:
At an international finance and economics conference in Bamako, Mali, Joao Almeida of Brazil and Lucinda Menon of India are discussing how to spur their countries’ economic growth. Almeida believes that growth can be bolstered by removing institutional impediments and suggests several possibilities for Brazil: launching a rural literacy program, clarifying property rights laws, and implementing a new dividend tax on foreign investors.

Menon responds that for India, capital deepening will be more effective, and she has proposed the following ideas: building a group of auto and textile factories in the southern states, developing a north–south and east–west highway network, and sponsoring a patent initiative.

In response, Almeida says to Menon:

“Based on endogenous growth theory, one of those proposals is more likely to raise total factor productivity than result in pure capital deepening.”

Although Menon recognizes that India lacks the significant natural resources that Brazil has, she states that India can overcome this challenge by bolstering long-term growth through three channels:

Channel 1	Deepening the capital base
Channel 2	Making investments in technology
Channel 3	Maintaining a low rupee exchange rate
Each country’s basic economic statistics were presented at the conference. Selected data for Brazil and India are presented in Exhibit 1. Adama Konaté, a fund manager based in Mali, is planning to increase the fund’s allocation to international equities and, after some preliminary analysis, has determined the new allocation will be to Brazilian or Indian equities. After reviewing the data in Exhibit 1, Konaté decides that the allocation will be to Indian equities.

Exhibit 1
Economic Statistics for Brazil and India
Economic Statistic	Brazil	India
GDP per capita, 2018	$14,360	$6,999
GDP per capita growth, 2000–2018	1.3%	5.8%
GDP growth, 2005–2018	2.0%	7.2%
- Growth resulting from labor productivity component	1.3%	6.3%
- Growth resulting from capital deepening component	1.9%	4.5%
Konaté is concerned about the low standard of living in Mali and its large informal sector. To improve per capita GDP, Konaté is considering five specific strategies:

Strategy 1

Lower the country’s tax rate.

Strategy 2

Introduce policies that encourage the return of highly educated Malian emigrants.

Strategy 3

Build daycare centers to increase women’s participation in the workforce.

Strategy 4

Impose high tariffs on imports to protect the country’s nascent industries.

Strategy 5

Use economic development bank loans to improve the country’s transport and manufacturing infrastructure.

questions.q: Which of Almeida’s initiatives is least likely to achieve his stated growth objective?
questions.why: B is correct. Almeida’s initiative to implement a new dividend tax is likely to impede inflows of equity capital by making equity investment in Brazil less attractive for foreign investors. Capital flows, or lack thereof, have a major impact on economic growth because, in an open economy, world savings can finance domestic investment. As a potential source of funds, foreign investment breaks the vicious cycle of low income, low domestic savings, and low investment.

questions.q: Which proposal for India is Almeida most likely referring to in his response to Menon?
questions.why: C is correct. Menon’s proposal to sponsor a patent initiative, which is likely to result in technology investment and improvement, is likely to cause a proportional upward shift in the entire production function, allowing the economy to produce higher output per worker for a given level of capital per worker. Technological progress also increases the marginal product of capital relative to its marginal cost.

questions.q: The channel that is least likely to help India overcome its challenge of lacking significant natural resources is:
questions.why: C is correct. Maintaining a low currency exchange rate is a policy aimed at maintaining demand for the country’s exports. It would have little direct impact on the potential growth rate of aggregate supply. It might boost long-term capacity growth indirectly, however, by encouraging adoption of leading edge technology. Nonetheless, it would not be expected to be as powerful as capital deepening and/or investment in technology.

questions.q: Based on Exhibit 1, which Indian economic statistic least likely supports Konaté’s international equity allocation preference?
questions.why: B is correct. Konaté’s decision to invest in equities in India is supported by the country’s strong economic growth. For global investors, economic growth is important because equity composite valuations depend to a great extent on both the level of economic output (GDP per capita and GDP overall) and the rate of economic growth. Relative to Brazil, India’s growth rate in per capita GDP has been much higher, and furthermore, the growth rate in GDP has also been much higher than that of Brazil. In contrast to the growth rate, the relatively low level of GDP per capita in India is less likely to indicate attractive equity investment opportunities. Low per capita GDP suggests that India may lack sufficient industrial and financial infrastructure to support some types of industries. It also indicates that domestic purchasing power is relatively limited, decreasing the potential for higher-margin, domestically oriented businesses.

title: Winslow: Dorado Beverages growth by acquisition, earnings quality and segments
body:
Natalie Wexford is an analyst working for Bright Impact Investments (HII), which manages a variety of investment funds. She analyzes the recent performance of Azulejo Beverages SA (DB), a multinational brewer of carbonated beverages that recently entered the energy drinks market. As a core holding, DB's prominence in Europe provides geographic diversification for HII which tends to be North-America-centric. 
Wexford refers to DB's most recent year and previous year balance sheets and comments: "DB is continuing to follow a growth-by-acquisition strategy." In addition, Wexford adjusts DB's most recent year income statement to determine the company's net income under the direct control of management by using information (in EUR millions) in Exhibit 1.
Exhibit 1
 	Most Recent Year
Income from operations	1,765
Income from investments in associates	191
Interest expense	(648)
Taxes	(238)
Net income	1,070
Of which:
Net income attributable to non-controlling interests	86
Net income attributable to shareholders	984
Wexford and her team assess the quality of DB's overall performance. The consensus is positive, but Wexford disagrees with her team for the following reasons:
Reason 1: The rate of fluctuation in the cash-flow-based accruals ratio is low.
Reason 2: Balance-sheet-based accruals are trending down relative to total assets.
Reason 3: Income from operations is consistently higher than cash generated from operations.
Wexford and her team notice from DB's annual report that the company has four segments. They analyze DB's segments by using information (in EUR millions) in Exhibit 2.
Exhibit 2
 	Most Recent Year	Previous Year
 	Sales	EBIT	Assets	Sales
Carbonated drinks - Europe	2,845	955	12,416	2,758
Carbonated drinks - North America	1,913	558	5,876	1,721
Carbonated drinks - Asia Pacific	535	172	2,661	503
Energy drinks	284	16	1,219	202
Total	5,577	1,701	22,172	5,184
After performing the segment analysis, Wexford and her team conclude on the following statements:
Statement 1: The sales growth rate in carbonated drinks - North America is stronger than that of energy drinks.
Statement 2: Carbonated drinks - Europe's EBIT margin is superior to that of carbonated drinks - North America. 
Statement 3: Asset turnover in carbonated drinks - Europe is better than that of DB overall.

questions.q: Which of the following balance sheet line items is most appropriate to justify Wexford's comment about DB's growth strategy?
questions.why: A. Incorrect because although property, plant and equipment may have changed (likely increased) as a result of a growth-by-acquisition strategy, it may also have changed because of significant new direct investments in capital. In addition, the nature of DB's industry suggests that acquisitions may include significant intangible assets (e.g., brands) that would not significantly change DB's property, plant and equipment. | B. Incorrect because although long-term debt may have changed (likely increased) as a result of a growth-by-acquisition strategy, it may also have changed because of changes to the target capital structure or a share-based acquisition strategy. | C. Correct because goodwill arises when a company acquires another business. Goodwill and intangible assets are hallmarks of a growth-by-acquisition strategy.

questions.q: After Wexford's adjustment, DB's net income (in EUR millions) under management's direct control is:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because this answer is net income attributable to shareholders which incorrectly includes income from investments in associates but incorrectly excludes net income attributable to non-controlling interests: Net income	1,070 Less: Net income attributable to non-controlling interests	   (86) Net income attributable to shareholders	984 Including the net investments and returns of associates with the full reported value of Nestlé’s own assets and income would introduce noise into the analytical signals. The returns earned by associates are not under the direct control of Nestlé’s management. | B. Incorrect because it correctly excludes income from investments in associates but incorrectly excludes net income attributable to non-controlling interests. Net income attributable to shareholders 	984 Less: Income from investments in associates	(191) 793 Including the net investments and returns of associates with the full reported value of Nestlé’s own assets and income would introduce noise into the analytical signals. The returns earned by associates are not under the direct control of Nestlé’s management. | C. Correct because it excludes the income from investments in associates which is not under DB's direct control (in EUR millions): Net income	1,070 Less: Income from investments in associates	 (191) 879 Including the net investments and returns of associates with the full reported value of Nestlé’s own assets and income would introduce noise into the analytical signals. The returns earned by associates are not under the direct control of Nestlé’s management.

questions.q: Which of the following reasons best supports Wexford's disagreement with her team about DB's overall performance?
questions.why: A. Incorrect because it is upward-trending relative accruals that could suggest management is trying to manipulate reported performance. Downward trending accruals provide less opportunity for manipulation. The analyst notes that the absolute level of accruals on the balance sheet is minor relative to the size of the operating assets, on either an ending balance basis or an average basis. The analyst would have been more concerned if the absolute levels of the accruals ratio were high; even more worrisome would have been if they were consistently trending higher. | B. Correct because the quality of income from operations is considered better when it is backed by cash flow. In this case, cash generated from operations is not fully backing income from operations, thereby calling the quality of income from operations into question. If the cash flow generated by operations was significantly or consistently less than operating profit, one would have reason to be suspicious about the quality of the operating profit. | C. Incorrect because a pattern of steady cash-flow-based accruals is unlikely to raise concerns. An erratic or upward-moving trend in cash-flow-based accruals would be concerning. The analyst would have been more concerned if the absolute levels of the accruals ratio were high; even more worrisome would have been if they were consistently trending higher.

title: Nkomo: residual income, MVA and fade
body:
Mandla Ncube, CFA, a senior equity analyst with Ellison-Brandt Investments, South Africa, has been assigned a recent graduate, Mpho Maseko, to assist in valuations. Maseko is interested in pursuing a career in equity analysis. In their first meeting, Ncube and Maseko discuss the concept of residual income and its commercial applications. Ncube asks Maseko to determine the market value added for a hypothetical South African firm using the data provided in Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1
Hypothetical Firm Data (amounts in South African rand)
Current share price	R25.43
Book value per share	R20.00
Total shares outstanding	30 million
Cost of equity	13%
Market value of debt	R55 million
Accounting book value of total capital	R650 million
Intrinsic share value of equity derived from residual income model	R22.00
Ncube also shares his valuation report of the hypothetical firm with Maseko. Ncube’s report concludes that the intrinsic value of the hypothetical firm, based on the residual income model, is R22.00 per share. To assess Maseko’s knowledge of residual income valuation, Ncube asks Maseko two questions about the hypothetical firm:

Question 1:
What conclusion can we make about future residual earnings given the current book value per share and my estimate of intrinsic value per share?

Question 2:
Suppose you estimated the intrinsic value of a firm’s shares using a constant growth residual income model, and you found that your estimate of intrinsic value equaled the book value per share. What would that finding imply about that firm’s return on equity?

Satisfied with Maseko’s response, Ncube requests that Maseko use the single-stage residual income model to determine the intrinsic value of the equity of Dawson Breweries, a brewery and bottling company, using data provided in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2
Dawson Breweries Data (amounts in South African rand)
Constant long-term growth rate	9.5%
Constant long-term ROE	13%
Current market price per share	R150.70
Book value per share	R55.81
Cost of equity	11%
Ncube also wants to update an earlier valuation of Brownstone, a food retailer. The valuation report, completed at the end of 2020, concluded an intrinsic value per share of R11.00 for Brownstone. The share price at that time was R8.25. Ncube points out to Maseko that in late 2020, Brownstone announced a significant restructuring charge, estimated at R2 million, that would be reported as part of operating earnings in Brownstone’s 2020 annual income statement. Ncube asks Maseko the following question about the restructuring charge:

Question 3:
What was the correct way to treat the estimated R2 million restructuring charge in my 2020 valuation report?

Satisfied with Maseko’s response, Ncube mentions to Maseko that Brownstone recently (near the end of 2021) completed the acquisition of a chain of convenience stores. Ncube requests that Maseko complete, as of the beginning of 2022, an updated valuation of Brownstone under two scenarios:

Scenario 1:
Estimate the value of Brownstone shares using a multistage residual income model with the data provided in Exhibit 3. Under Scenario 1, expected ROE in 2025 is 26%, but it is assumed that the firm’s ROE will slowly decline towards the cost of equity thereafter.

Scenario 2:
Estimate the value of Brownstone shares using a multistage residual income model with the data provided in Exhibit 3, but assume that at the end of 2024, share price is expected to equal book value per share.

Scenario 3:
Exhibit 3
Brownstone Data (amounts in South African rand)
Long-term growth rate starting in 2025	9.0%
Expected ROE in 2025	26%
Current market price per share	R16.55
Book value per share, beginning of 2022	R7.60
Cost of equity	10%
Persistence factor	0.70
  

 	2022	2023	2024
Expected earnings per share	R3.28	R3.15	R2.90
Expected dividend per share	R2.46	R2.36	R2.06

questions.q: Based on the information in Exhibit 1, the market value added of the hypothetical firm is closest to:
questions.why:
A is correct. Market value added equals the market value of firm minus total accounting book value of total capital.
Market value added = Market value of company – Accounting book value of total capital
Market value of firm = Market value of debt + Market value of equity
Market value of firm = R55 million + (30,000,000 × R25.43)
Market value of firm = R55 million + R762.9 million = R817.9 million
Market value added = R817.9 million – R650 million = R167.9 million, or approximately R168 million.

questions.q: The most appropriate response to Ncube’s Question 1 would be that the present value of future residual earnings is expected to be:
questions.why: B is correct. The intrinsic value of R22.00 is greater than the current book value of R20.00. The residual income model states that the intrinsic value of a stock is its book value per share plus the present value of expected (future) per share residual income. The higher intrinsic value per share, relative to book value per share, indicates that the present value of expected per share residual income is positive.

questions.q: The most appropriate response to Ncube’s Question 2 would be that the firm’s return on equity is:
options: equal to the firm’s cost of equity.
higher than the firm’s cost of equity.
lower than the firm’s cost of equity.
questions.why: A is correct because the intrinsic value is the book value per share, B0,plus the expected residual income stream, or B0 + [(ROE – r)B0/(r – g)]. If ROE equals the cost of equity (r), then V0 = B0. This implies that ROE is equal to the cost of the equity, and therefore there is no residual income contribution to the intrinsic value. As a result, intrinsic value would be equal to book value.

questions.q: Based on the information in Exhibit 2, the intrinsic value per share of the equity of Dawson Breweries is closest to:
questions.why: C is correct. With a single-stage residual income (RI) model, the intrinsic value, V0, is calculated assuming a constant return on equity (ROE) and a constant earnings growth (g).

title: ETFs · Provident Advisers: authorized participants, tracking error, completion strategies, smart beta
body:
Prudent Advisers is a registered investment advisory firm that uses exchange-traded funds (ETFs) for its clients’ investment portfolios. Tom Sorensen is CEO and chief investment officer of Prudent. Steve Marlow, a prospective client, is a high-net-worth individual who is considering transforming his actively managed portfolio of individual stocks and bonds into actively managed and passive ETFs. Marlow is considering this strategy because of the advice of his accountant, Andrew Holt. Sorensen, Marlow, and Holt are meeting to discuss ETFs and their growing use in the construction of investment portfolios.

Sorensen begins the meeting by describing how ETFs are subject to the same regulations as mutual funds and noting that ETFs trade intra-day, similar to public stocks. Holt adds that ETF authorized participants use the primary market to both create and redeem ETF shares, and the secondary market to conduct trades in ETFs to eliminate the arbitrage gap.

Marlow asks Sorensen to describe how ETF performance is measured. Sorensen explains that most ETFs are designed to track the performance of a specific benchmark index, such as the S&P 500 Index. Sorensen cautions, however, that there are numerous sources of tracking error that may cause a deviation in an ETF’s return relative to its benchmark index. Sorensen provides an example, stating that one of the sources of tracking error is an ETF portfolio manager’s operations with short sellers.

Marlow wants to maintain the current blended stock and bond benchmark allocations following his portfolio’s transition from individual stocks and bonds to active and passive ETFs. Sorensen states that whenever active ETF managers implement active views, gaps with respect to desired market exposures may result. For Marlow’s portfolio, Sorensen plans to use passive ETFs to maintain benchmark exposure should any of the active ETF managers implement active views that cause changes in the portfolio’s industry sector weightings. Passive ETFs will enable Sorensen to maintain benchmark exposure while not necessarily replacing an active ETF manager.

Holt states that active ETF strategies have evolved such that market capitalization is no longer the only benchmark factor for equity strategies and that fixed-income strategies may be constructed with minimal sensitivity to movements in interest rates. He states that smart beta equity risk factors, such as dividend yield, size, value, and momentum, enable investors to implement an active view while continuing to track a designated benchmark. He then describes the strategy of smart beta fixed-income ETFs that focus on generating returns from taking credit risk and hedging out duration risk.

questions.q: Is Holt’s statement about ETF authorized participants most likely correct?
options: No, regarding their use of the primary markets
No, regarding their trades in the secondary markets
questions.why: A. Incorrect. Holt’s statement that ETF authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares in the primary markets is correct. | B. Incorrect. Holt’s statement is incorrect. ETF authorized participants do not trade in the secondary market. ETF authorized participants create and redeem shares in the primary market. | C. Correct. Holt’s statement about authorized participants is not correct because of trades in the secondary market. ETF secondary market trades are transactions between buyers and sellers of existing ETF shares. No new ETF shares are created by trades in the secondary market. ETF authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares in the primary market.

questions.q: In describing tracking error, Sorensen’s example most likely relates to:
questions.why: A. Incorrect. Replication (lack of full replication) is a source of tracking error but is not caused by operations with short sellers. | B. Correct. Sorensen’s description of ETF tracking error includes a reference to securities lending by the ETF portfolio manager. Many ETF portfolio managers lend a portion of their portfolio holdings to short sellers. Securities lending provides income for an ETF that offsets a portion of an ETF’s administrative expenses. | C. Incorrect. Trading costs are a source of tracking error but are not caused by operations with short sellers.

questions.q: Sorensen’s explanation of benchmark exposure most likely describes portfolio:
questions.why: A. Incorrect. Sorensen’s explanation describes completion strategies, not portfolio rebalancing. Portfolio rebalancing describes how ETFs are used by investors to remain fully invested according to target weights whenever changes in market values cause a portfolio’s segments to deviate from target weights. | B. Correct. Sorensen’s explanation of benchmark exposure describes portfolio completion. ETFs can be used to fill a temporary gap in exposure to an asset class. Gaps may arise whenever an active manager transitions a portfolio away from a desired market exposure (for example, the portfolio’s benchmark). An investor may use a passive ETF to maintain the exposure while retaining the manager. | C. Incorrect. Sorensen’s explanation describes completion strategies, not portfolio liquidity management. Portfolio liquidity management describes how ETFs are used by investors to efficiently invest excess cash balances, which reduces a portfolio’s cash drag.

questions.q: Is Holt’s comments about active ETF strategies most likely correct?
options: No, because of the comment about smart beta equity risk factors
No, because of the comment about smart beta fixed-income ETFs
questions.why: A. Incorrect. Holt’s comment about smart beta equity risk factors is correct. | B. Incorrect. Holt’s comment about smart beta fixed-income ETFs is correct. | C. Correct. Holt’s comments about smart beta are correct. Factor (smart beta) ETFs are benchmarked to an index created with predefined rules for screening and weighting constituent holdings whose index rules are structured around return drivers, or factors, such as dividend yield, size, value, and momentum. Academic research has supported these factors as contributors to the equity risk premium. Holt’s comment about smart beta fixed-income ETFs is correct. Interest rate swaps are used by the managers of smart beta fixed-income ETFs to minimize interest rate risk, enabling the ETFs’ return to be generated by taking credit risk.

title: Arnie Burr: Princeton Capital
body:
Arnold Birch is CEO and chief investment officer of Plymouth Capital, a registered investment advisory firm. He is working with Tom Jeffries, head trader, and Jim Maddox, a new analyst. They meet to discuss option valuation methodologies in the context of the firm’s use of derivatives to manage client portfolios.

Birch begins the discussion by stating that the Black–Scholes–Merton (BSM) model is a relatively straightforward tool for valuing options despite its rigorous computational components. Birch writes the BSM model on the firm’s whiteboard, presented as Exhibit 1.

Exhibit 1: BSM Model for Options on Non-Dividend Paying Stocks

c = SN(d1) – e^(–rT)XN(d2),
and
p = e^(–rT)XN(–d2) – SN(–d1),
where
d1 = [[ln(S/X) + (r + σ²/2)T|σ√T]] and d2 = d1 − σ√T.

(The definitions of d1 and d2 were missing from the copied text; the standard BSM definitions are shown.)

Birch wants to assess Maddox’s comprehension of the components of the BSM. Maddox states that a call option can be viewed as a leveraged position in the underlying stock. To replicate a call option, the appropriate strategy is to purchase N(d1) shares and simultaneously borrow an amount e^(–rT)XN(–d2).

Jeffries introduces option Greeks into the conversation, stating, “The BSM model contains six inputs: the stock price, the option’s exercise price, dividends, the risk-free interest rate, time to maturity, and implied volatility. The effect of the BSM model inputs on the price of an option can be measured by the option Greeks. Delta and gamma are measures of the relationship between a change in the stock price and the option price. Theta is a measure that typically approaches zero at an increasing rate as the option approaches maturity. Holding all other factors constant, Vega is a measure that typically is higher whenever an option is “out of the money.”

Birch states that a client would like to sell calls on 1,000 shares of Weston stock. Stock and option information on Weston stock is presented in Exhibit 2.

Exhibit 2: Option Information on Weston Corporation Stock
	
Stock Price	$100
Call Option Exercise Price	$100
Call Option Value	$9.23
Call Option Delta	0.587
Call Option Gamma	0.019

Birch asks Maddox to outline an appropriate hedging strategy. Maddox replies that to be fully hedged, an option trader will need to consider how changes in the stock price relative to the option exercise price affect the value of the call options. To be fully hedged against a small change in the stock price, Maddox suggests that the proper strategy to construct the hedge is to use call option delta and add the call option gamma to arrive at the number of shares required.

Maddox notes that the implied volatility for the Weston call option outlined in Exhibit 2 is 30%. With respect to other call options on Weston stock, Maddox states the volatility surface provides a visualization of how implied volatility varies across both exercise price and time to maturity. Birch adds that implied volatility is useful in assessing the market price of risk since it is calculated on the basis of the historical volatility in the stock price. Jeffries concurs and adds that the volatility smile and skew typically have identical shapes whenever the market price of hedging is rising.

questions.q: Maddox’s statement about the BSM model is least likely correct with respect to:
options: the leveraged position in a stock.
questions.why: A call is a leveraged stock position: buy N(d1) shares and BORROW e^(−rT) X N(d2), which is exactly the second term of c = S N(d1) − e^(−rT) X N(d2). The amount e^(−rT) X N(−d2) is what is LENT when replicating a put (p = e^(−rT) X N(−d2) − S N(−d1)). B and A are correct parts of his statement.

questions.q: Jeffries’s statement about option Greeks is least likely correct with respect to:
questions.why: Vega (sensitivity to volatility) is HIGHEST for options at or near the money and lower when they are deep in or out of the money, so his vega claim is wrong. B is wrong: theta (time decay) does behave as he describes, changing at an increasing rate as expiry nears. C is wrong: delta and gamma do both measure how the option responds to changes in the stock price.

questions.q: Is Maddox’s suggested hedging strategy for Weston options most likely correct?
options: No, he should only use delta
questions.why:
Per the source answer: delta (0.587) shows how many shares hedge one call now, and gamma (0.019) shows how much delta changes for a $1 move in the stock. Adding them, 0.587 + 0.019 = 0.606 shares per call, anticipates the new delta after a small rise in the stock. B is wrong: gamma is added, not subtracted.
Note: in the standard curriculum a plain delta hedge uses delta alone, and gamma risk is neutralized with other options, not shares. Treat this answer as specific to this question.

questions.q: Whose comment regarding implied volatility is most likely correct?
questions.why: Maddox is right: the volatility surface shows implied volatility across both exercise prices and maturities. C is wrong: implied volatility is backed out from MARKET option prices and reflects expected FUTURE volatility; it is not calculated from historical volatility. A is wrong: when demand for hedging rises, the skew steepens, so its shape differs from the smile; they don't become identical.

title: Zhang: Arbitrage Partners, arbitrage-free valuation and tree construction
body:
Dennis Zhou is a fixed-income analyst at Equilibrium Partners, a hedge fund focusing on global macro arbitrage opportunities. The fixed-income team focuses on securities issued in developing markets that trade in multiple world financial centers. Zhou is conducting a training session for a new analyst, John Hollis.

Zhou explains: “Our fixed-income team focuses on constructing a portfolio of fixed-income securities issued in local markets that trade in multiple markets around the world. We seek out securities we believe to be mispriced and identify these using an arbitrage-free approach to valuation, which can be described as follows. The cash flows of any fixed-income security can be thought of as a package of separate zero-coupon bonds. Each zero-coupon bond in such a package is valued separately at a discount rate corresponding to the interest rate on the yield curve at the time of the cash flow.

When the present values of the coupon payments are summed and added to the present value of the principal payment at maturity, the result should equal the current price of the bond. In order to calculate the arbitrage-free value of a bond, we determine the future coupon and principal payments for the bond. If the yield curve is positively sloped, the appropriate interest rate used to discount each cash flow will be different. However, in the event the yield curve is flat, all cash flows will be discounted in the same manner as in the traditional approach to valuing bonds.”

Hollis comments: “Last year, South Africa issued multiple two-year and four-year Green Bonds denominated in US dollars with annual coupons. The four-year bonds were callable, while the two-year bonds had no embedded options.

I recall an example of an arbitrage opportunity of the two-year bonds trading in different global financial centers. The benchmark yield curve, bond coupon rates, and bond prices are shown in Exhibits 1 and 2.”

Exhibit 1 Benchmark Interest Rates
Maturity (years)	Coupon Rate	Spot Rate	1-Year Implied Forward Rate
1	5.00%	5%	5.00% (current)
2	5.97%	6%	7.01%
3	6.91%	7%	9.03%
4	7.81%	8%	11.06%

Exhibit 2 Bond Price Quotes
Market	Coupon Rate	Quoted Price
Dubai	1%	90.842
Shanghai	2%	92.684
New York	4%	94.630

Zhou adds: “While your example represents good practice, we also need to be able to value bonds with embedded options where expected cash flows of bonds with options change depending on the path of future interest rates. We typically construct an interest rate tree as a visual representation of the paths of future interest rates, with the average of possible future values being centered on the current yield curve. The following three steps can be employed to construct an interest rate tree for valuing a particular bond:

Step 1: Using prices of the benchmark bonds, determine the current par curve.
Step 2: Estimate interest rate volatility, and calculate the potential paths of future rates.
Step 3: Starting with the current market price, calculate each successive node’s value.

The interest rate tree must then be calibrated to fit the actual yield curve while being consistent with an underlying interest rate model.”

Hollis states: “I believe the iterative process must involve a trial-and-error search to determine the higher and lower rates subsequent to each node in the tree, which branches out from an average yield centered on the forward rate curve. The rates must also be consistent with an assumption of log-normality, the volatility assumption, and the observed market value of the bond being evaluated.”

questions.q: Is Zhou most likely correct in his description of calculating the arbitrage-free approach to fixed-income security valuation?
options: No, with respect to the discount rate used with a positively sloped yield curve.
No, with respect to the discount rate used with a flat yield curve.
questions.why: With a positively sloped curve each cash flow is discounted at a different (higher for later) spot rate; with a flat curve the same rate applies to all, as in the traditional approach.

questions.q: According to the data in Exhibits 1 and 2, in which trading location is the bond most likely mispriced?
questions.why: Discounting at the spot rates gives 90.842 (Dubai) and 92.684 (Shanghai), equal to their quotes. The 4%-coupon bond in New York has an arbitrage-free value above its quote of 94.630, so it is underpriced.

questions.q: Which of Zhou’s three steps to value bonds with embedded options is least likely correct?
questions.why: Node values are found by backward induction starting from the known value at maturity, not by starting with the current market price.

questions.q: When describing calibrating the interest rate tree, Hollis is least likely correct with respect to the:
options: value of the bond being evaluated.
questions.why: Calibration depends on a volatility assumption, an interest rate model (here log-normality) and the observed market values of the benchmark bonds, not the bond being evaluated.

source: Mock paper 6 (rebuilt 7 Nov from stored vignettes that had not appeared in any earlier mock; names changed, options reordered)
title: Ethics · Kostecka: Bope account and Jabbertalk IPO
body:
Jacob Kowalski, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Harlan Investment Management, an asset management and research focused organization. After obtaining his CFA charter last month, Kowalski was transferred to the private wealth management division at Harlan.

Dhruv Bapat, a private wealth client, was involved in a major motorcycle accident and is in critical condition, fighting for his life. Bapat is a single parent with a daughter, Pavan Naidoo, in her mid-twenties. Since the accident, Naidoo has managed her father’s affairs, paying all expenses, including investment advisory fees. In several conversations with Naidoo, Kowalski highlighted Bapat’s low risk tolerance and investment goal of capital preservation. Naidoo has indicated her interest in managing the account more aggressively and possibly moving to another management firm. Naidoo recently petitioned the court to appoint her full power of attorney to legally manage Bapat’s affairs. Prior to the court decision, Naidoo asks Kowalski to invest her father’s account in the initial public offering (IPO) of Bluechirp, a highly sought after social media company that has yet to generate a profit.

The following week, the court approves Naidoo’s request to act on behalf of her father.

Naidoo establishes a non-discretionary investment account at Harlan tied to her newly established business. Shortly thereafter, Kowalski joins the board of Talkwave.com, a smaller social media competitor to Bluechirp. Based on his knowledge of Bluechirp, Kowalski believes the stock of Talkwave is a good investment, even though it is not yet profitable. Buoyed by his faith in social media, Kowalski ultimately purchases shares of Talkwave’s IPO for Naidoo’s account, as well as for all clients he currently manages. When Kowalski informs Naidoo of the purchase, she expresses concern about her legal responsibilities and lack of accounting knowledge in overseeing the account. Kowalski provides Naidoo a list of recommended professionals he has worked with in the past, including attorneys and accountants. When he was in college 10 years earlier, Kowalski was engaged to one of the attorneys but broke off the relationship prior to their wedding, and one of the accountants was Kowalski’s college roommate. Since then, Kowalski has not had any contact with the lawyer and accountant.

The Talkwave investment is profitable on the first day of trading, doubling from its opening price. Kowalski tells his clients the multifactor valuation model used by Harlan shows Talkwave stock is still undervalued. Harlan’s research report, due out the next day, will recommend investors hold their Talkwave shares. However, Kowalski tells all his clients simultaneously they should sell their shares because he believes Talkwave is overvalued and the stock price will fall soon. Kowalski notes he has followed through on this belief by selling his personal holdings of Talkwave shares. Naidoo ignores Kowalski’s recommendation to sell Talkwave. Over the next week, the stock declines 75%.

Watching Talkwave’s severe share price decline, Naidoo becomes furious with Kowalski because he did not sell shares of Talkwave in her account. She files a complaint with Kowalski’s supervisor, Sally Feng, CFA, claiming she was misled on the value of the IPO in the days immediately after the stock started trading. Kowalski responds to the complaint by telling Feng, “the analyst who wrote the hold recommendation on Talkwave has only passed his CFA Level II examination. As a charterholder, I have earned the right to use the CFA designation, so I am more qualified to manage clients’ investments.”

questions.q: With regard to the investment request made by Naidoo to invest in Bluechirp, Kowalski should most likely:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because the account should still be managed as the client requested since the daughter has not yet been granted legal responsibility over her father’s affairs by the court. An investment in an IPO of an unprofitable social networking company most likely does not meet the father’s investment goal. | B. Correct. The account should be managed according to the client’s investment goal of capital preservation and a low risk tolerance. Under Standard III(A) –Loyalty, Prudence, and Care, the first step for members and candidates in fulfilling their duty of loyalty to clients is to determine the identity of the “client” to whom the duty of loyalty is owed. Only when the daughter is granted legal responsibility over her father’s affairs by the court does she become the client. | C. Incorrect because the account should still be managed as the client requested, an investment goal of capital preservation and a low risk tolerance. An investment in an IPO of an unprofitable social networking company most likely does not meet Bapat’s investment goal. Since the daughter has not yet been granted legal responsibility over her father’s affairs by the court, the adviser is not required to follow through on this request.

questions.q: With regard to investing in Talkwave and recommending experts, Kowalski most likely needs to disclose conflicts related to his:
questions.why: A. Incorrect because even though one of the accountants Kowalski recommended is his college roommate, this is only one of several individuals he recommended and it is not a basic conflict of interest, which needs to be disclosed. | B. Incorrect because even though Kowalski was previously engaged to one of the attorneys, the relationship ended a decade ago and it is unlikely that this relationship poses a potential conflict of interest at this time. | C. Correct. Kowalski’s board service creates the opportunity to receive material nonpublic information involving Talkwave and is a basic conflict of interest. As a result, according to Standard VI(A)–Conflicts of Interest, the directorship should be disclosed. Members and candidates must make full and fair disclosure of all matters that could reasonably be expected to impair their independence and objectivity or interfere with respective duties to their clients, prospective clients, and their employer. Because the member has not made any disclosure concerning his board membership, he is in violation of Standard VI(A). Kowalski has also ignored his clients mandate of low risk tolerance and capital preservation and is in violation of Standard III(C)–Suitability. In addition, Naidoo has violated her fiduciary duty as a “trustee” of the account as she failed to manage her father’s portfolio in accordance with his wishes.

questions.q: In relation to Kowalski’s handling of the Talkwave stock recommendation, which of the following CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct did he least likely violate?
questions.why: A. Incorrect because according to Standard V(B)–Communication with Clients and Prospective Clients, Kowalski should have distinguished fact from opinion. In addition, Kowalski should also disclose to clients and prospective clients the basic format and general principles of the investment processes used to analyze investments, select securities, and construct portfolios and must promptly disclose any changes that might materially affect those processes and use reasonable judgment in identifying which factors are important to his investment analyses, recommendations, or actions and include those factors in communications with clients and prospective clients. | B. Incorrect because Kowalski has violated Standard VI(B)–Priority of Transactions. There is a potential conflict of interest because the client and the adviser hold the same stock, so the client should be given first priority to trade Talkwave. | C. Correct. Standard III(B)–Fair Dealing requires members and candidates to deal fairly and objectively with all clients when providing investment analysis, making investment recommendations, taking investment action, or engaging in other professional activities. When Kowalski informs clients of the upcoming investment recommendation by Harlan, he has treated all clients fairly because this disclosure is provided to all of his current clients.

questions.q: When Kowalski defends himself against Naidoo’s complaint, he most likely violated the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct concerning the:
options: reference to candidacy in the CFA Program.
right to use the CFA designation.
misrepresentation of the meaning of the designation.
questions.why: A. Incorrect because he properly references his colleague as a Level II candidate. | B. Incorrect because there is no indication that Kowalski does not have the right to use the CFA designation especially since he recently received his charter. | C. Correct. Statements overstating the competency of an individual or imply, either directly or indirectly, that superior performance can be expected from someone with the CFA designation are not allowed under Standard VII(B)–Reference to CFA Institute, the CFA Designation, and the CFA Program. The Standard specifically states that when referring to CFA Institute, CFA Institute membership, the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program, members and candidates must not misrepresent or exaggerate the meaning or implications of membership in the CFA Institute, holding the CFA designation, or candidacy in the CFA Program.
